In this paper, we investigate the sources of tin in 153 tin and bronze samples from south- ern Africa, dated between 1200 and 1800 CE, by integrating lead isotope, tin iso- tope, and trace element measurements. Our data show that tin from the prehistoric tin mines at Rooiberg (South Africa) was transported more than 900 km. We also present evidence of tin production from other sources, likely pegmatites, within the Bushveld Large Igneous Province of South Africa. Although many of the bronzes analyzed are from archaeological sites in present Zimbabwe, we have found no defi- nite evidence so far for exploitation of tin sources within Zimbabwe. Rare examples of forged iron meteorites are known from Egypt as early as 3200 BCE (Rehren et al., 2013). To the south of the Sahara, the sequence is completely different, except in Nubia and in regions adjacent to the Red Sea. Smelted iron and cop- per were the first metals used, usually approximately simultaneously. These first appeared in the early to mid-first millennium BCE in the Sahel, and spread gradu- ally southwards, only reaching southern Africa in the early centuries CE (Killick, 2016). Lead, silver, gold, tin, and bronze are essentially absent from archaeologi- cal sites in sub-Saharan Africa dating before 800 CE, when Muslim traders devel- oped long-distance routes into the interior from the Mediterranean and from the coast of East Africa. These five metals are only found before 1500 CE in regions that were connected to Muslim intercontinental trade (Herbert, 1984; Killick, 2016), and of these, only gold, tin, and bronze were actually produced by Afri- can metallurgists. Lead is very rarely reported from sites in the African interior. We discuss below two fourteenth/fifteenth century lead–tin alloys from southern Africa that were likely produced accidentally during the smelting of tin ores, but there is no evidence for deliberate smelting of lead, or for recovery of silver from lead ores by cupellation, until Portuguese colonists used them in the seventeenth century to test potential silver sources in present Mozambique (Axelson, 1960: passim). These technologies did not then transfer to African artisans, and the deliberate smelting of lead in sub-Saharan Africa by African metallurgists is not documented until the nineteenth century (Rademakers et al., 2018). Silver is very rarely reported from archaeological sites in the interior of sub-Saharan Africa and was likely always imported. Although there are tin deposits in various parts of West Africa, Central Africa, and southern Africa (Kinnaird et al., 2016), tin mining and smelting by Africans was reported in only two locations by European colonists in the early twentieth century. The first was around the Jos Plateau of central Nigeria, where beads and wires of metallic tin were often found by prospectors working alluvial cassiterite deposits in the early twentieth century (Fell, 1939; King, 1989). There has been no archaeo- logical study of precolonial tin production in Nigeria, but the famous ninth-tenth century unleaded cast bronzes from Igbo Ukwu (McIntosh, 2022; Shaw, 1970) are assumed to have used tin from the Jos Plateau. The second location is the Rooiberg valley in northern South Africa, where early European prospectors found extensive evidence of hard-rock mining for cassiterite (Baumann, 1919; Recknagel, 1908). There is a large archaeological literature on Rooiberg (listed in Chirikure et al., 2023, 2024, and Miller & Hall, 2008). Current estimates are that at least 1000 tons of cassiterite were mined here, starting some- where between the tenth and thirteenth centuries, and ending around 1840. Impor- tantly, the tin mineral stannite (Cu FeSnS ) was not a target for these precolonial 2 4 miners, nor is it a component of most tin deposits reviewed in this paper. Techno- logical studies of tin smelting slags show that both alluvial and hard-rock mining of cassiterite was practiced (Chirikure et al., 2010). There is surprisingly little evi- dence of smelting near the mines. Chirikure et al. (2023, 2024) argue that the tin Complementary Use of Lead Isotopes, Tin Isotopes, and Trace… Page 3 of 60 6 mines were an open resource and that cassiterite mined there was carried away to be smelted in other places. The earliest bronzes currently documented in southern Africa are from Mapun- gubwe on the Limpopo River (the current border between South Africa and Zim- babwe) and date in the interval 1220–1300 CE (Miller, 2001). A recent campaign (2019–2022) of chemical and isotopic analysis of archaeological copper objects by two of us—JS and DK—found 153 bronzes in 339 analyzed samples. The great majority of these bronzes were from sites in present Zimbabwe and Botswana. This raises the issue of whether these were made with tin from Rooiberg, which is at least 400 km from sites in Botswana and Zimbabwe but is at present the only local- ity where there is archaeological evidence of precolonial tin mining. There are no tin sources in Botswana, but there are several in Zimbabwe, and several apart from Rooiberg in northern South Africa (Kinnaird et al., 2016). This study focuses on the methods that we have developed to infer the sources of tin artifacts, and of the tin in bronzes. The full archaeological implications of these data will be deferred to future articles, as will our inferences about the sources of copper used to make the bronzes. We begin with a discussion of the crystal chemis- try of cassiterite (SnO )—the only significant tin mineral found in southern Africa— 2 and of the geological processes that create tin ore deposits. These have important implications for the interpretation of lead isotope and tin isotope ratios, the data that we employ to infer the geological provenance of tin. We then discuss trace elements in cassiterite, and how concentrations and ratios of these elements should in theory be altered in the smelting of cassiterite to tin metal. After this, we list the tin ore deposits of southern Africa, with their geological ages and reported mineral invento- ries. This is followed by a brief review of prior work on precolonial tin mining and metallurgy in southern Africa, and of prior studies of the chemistry and lead iso- tope ratios of precolonial tin ingots. We then report the lead and tin isotopic ratios and chemical compositions that we have measured on archaeological tin objects and bronzes, and compare these to data for the tin sources. We focus in particular on the data for the 153 bronzes in our sample. The major question here is whether the lead from copper obscures the lead isotopic signatures of the added tin. To resolve ambi- guities in the lead isotope data, we obtained tin isotope data for 46 bronzes. Lastly, we present our general conclusions about the provenance and distribution of tin in precolonial southern Africa. Background: Lead Isotopic Ratios in Cassiterites Primary copper, lead, and silver minerals are sulfides, and their lead isotopic ratios are (barring metamorphic alteration) those locked in at the time of crystallization. It is generally assumed that the secondary weathering products (oxides, hydroxides, and carbonates) have the same isotopic ratios as their parent sulfide ores. Ideally, the lead isotope ratios for a single source are tightly clustered, so inference of the prov- enance of copper, lead, and silver artifacts is made by matching isotopic ratios of individual artifacts to the clusters of ratios obtained on ore minerals from potential sources (Pernicka, 2014). 6 Page 4 of 60 J. Stephens et al. The interpretation of lead isotopic ratios in southern African tin requires a very different approach (Killick et al., 2020; Molofsky et al., 2014; Powell et al., 2021). There are several sulfide tin minerals (all in the sulfostannate group), but these are extremely rare in southern Africa. Cassiterite ( SnO ) is the only tin mineral relevant 2 to our study. Unlike sulfide minerals, cassiterite can accommodate U4+ and Th4+ ions in its crystal lattice, both of which substitute for Sn4+ (Faure, 1998; Faure & Mensing, 2005). The radioactive isotopes of U and Th decay to lead isotopes— 238U to 206Pb, 235U to 207Pb, 232Th to 208Pb. Ratios of these daughter products to the primordial stable isotope 204Pb in cassiterite thus increase steadily (“evolve”) with time elapsed since crystallization. Initial Pb concentrations in cassiterite should be very low because of large differences in ionic radius and charge between Pb2+ and Sn4+. The present-day Pb isotopic ratios of cassiterite are therefore determined by (1) initial Pb concentration, (2) initial U and Th concentrations, and (3) time elapsed since crystallization. Pb isotopic ratios in cassiterite from a single mine may vary because of variation in initial U and Th concentrations in individual crystals of cas- siterite, but on a plot of 207Pb/204Pb against 206Pb/204Pb, all cassiterites from a sin- gle-stage deposit— one where there was only one period of mineralization—should fall on a straight line called an isochron, the slope of which is proportional to the geological age of the deposit (Faure & Mensing, 2005). Archaeological scientists have recently claimed to have identified isochrons in lead isotope ratios of archaeo- logical tin metal (e.g., Berger et al., 2019a; Molofsky et al., 2014). Although these lines have clear chronological significance, Powell et al. (2024) have noted that their Mean Square Weighted Deviation (MSWD) values greatly exceed those accepted by geochemists (MSWD < 3) for isochrons (Faure & Mensing, 2005), given the sample size in Molofsky et al. (2014) and Berger et al. (2019a). These lines are more cor- rectly termed errorchrons, and we adopt this term here. Provenance attribution for an individual tin artifact is done by comparing its measured lead isotope ratios to the errorchrons of potential tin sources (Molofsky et al., 2014). Cassiterite is notoriously insoluble in acids, so reliable measurements of Pb, U, and Th in this mineral have only been obtained since 2018 by laser ablation induc- tively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS). Powell et al. (2024) have compiled global data for cassiterite samples, ranging in age from 3068 to 60 Ma. Concentrations of U in tin deposits ranged from 1 to 223 ppm (μg g−1), with only the Yinyan (China) and Rooiberg (South Africa) tin deposits exceeding 100 ppm U. Pb was not measured on all samples, but where it was, concentrations ranged from 0.1 to 60 ppm, with only Precambrian deposits having Pb concentrations greater than 7.4 ppm. The concentration of Th ranges between 0.0 and 17.7 ppm, but almost all measured concentrations are below 0.5 ppm. Since T h4+ can in theory readily substitute for S n4+, its absence in cassiterite is attributed to the known insolubility of Th ions and complexes in the oxidized aqueous solutions that precipitate cassiterite. (Uranium-series dating exploits this same difference in solubility of uranium and thorium in oxygen-rich near-surface waters.) These measurements show that tin smelted from relatively young tin deposits will contain very little Pb derived from in-situ decay of U and thus will have a high potential for contamination from other sources of lead (Powell et al., 2024). There are however much older (Archean to Paleoproterozoic) tin sources in southern Africa and India. Two tin deposits from Swaziland are dated to 3.0 and 2.7 Ga (Trumbull, 1995); pegmatites at Bikita and Benson in Zimbabwe to 2.6 Ga (Melcher et al., 2015); and pegmatites in the Bastar-Malkangi belt in eastern central India to about 2.3 Ga (Pal et al., 2007). The LGS is dated to 2.05 Ga (Skursch et al., 2022). There are also Mesoproterozoic to Neoproterozoic Sn deposits in southern Africa and India. The Kamativi pegmatites in Zimbabwe are dated to 1.0 Ga (Melcher et al., 2015) and three eras of pegmatite formation between 1.29 and 0.95 Ga are documented in the Bihar Mica Belt of northwest India (Hazarika et al., 2017). (2021: Table 2). For comparison, cassiterite crystallized at 100 Ma (0.1 Ga)—near the start of the Mesozoic to Ceno- zoic orogeny that formed tin deposits across Eurasia from Italy to Myanmar—has 1.1–26.2 ppm U and 0.2–0.7 ppm Pb (Powell et al., 2024). These observations are again aligned with Powell et al. (2021: Table 2), who predict 0.8 ppm Pb from an initial U concentration of 50 ppm. The major archaeological implication of this review is that metallic tin produced from cassiterite in southern Africa and India should be clearly distinguishable by Pb concentration, and by 206Pb/204Pb and 207Pb/204Pb ratios, from tin produced in Europe and the rest of Asia. Fractionation of Pb isotope ratios during smelting can be discounted, as Cui and Feng (2011) have shown by experiment that even large percentage losses of Pb as vapor do not cause significant fractionation of Pb isotopic ratios in the remaining liquid. A more serious concern is that cassiterite ore deposits may contain minor amounts of galena (PbS). Sn and Pb are completely miscible when molten, so even a small grain of galena in the ore feed could skew the Pb isotope ratios of an entire Sn artifact. Powell et al. (2021) note “excess lead” – lead concentrations above those expected from decay of 238U and 235U—in more than half of the 117 tin ingots from the Late Bronze Age Uluburun shipwreck. Background: Tin Isotopic Ratios in Cassiterites Unlike lead isotopes, tin isotopes are not derived from the radioactive decay of unstable parent isotopes and are therefore not time dependent. Rather, they are stable isotopes whose ratios change based on changes in chemical and physical parameters (reviewed in Stephens et al., 2021). While archaeological studies have 6 Page 6 of 60 J. Stephens et al. attempted to use tin isotopes for inferences of provenance, their application ran far ahead of geological understandings for why tin isotopes fractionate (or change the ratio of heavy to light isotopes) in nature. New research shows that physicochemical factors related to tin mineralization are intrinsically linked to tin isotopic fractiona- tion, thus demonstrating the need to understand how tin ore deposits form. Primary tin deposits—those exploited by hard-rock mining—are divided into hydrothermal deposits and pegmatites. In both cases, the concentration of tin from the low levels typically present in granitic magmas is thought to be driven by fractional crystalliza- tion, whereby incompatible elements—those that do not readily fit into the crystal lattices of common rock-forming silicate minerals—are concentrated in the remain- ing liquid. Pegmatites form when the last silicate melt solidifies to form individual minerals, often of unusually large crystal sizes (Černý, 1991; Černý et al., 2005; London, 2008, 2018). Water, halogen ligands ( F−, Cl−, and Br−), and sulfur (S) are also concentrated in the magma remaining after crystallization of quartz and feld- spars from granitic magmas, as is boron (B). Higher concentrations of B and F allow silicate melts to hold more water in solution at lower temperatures (Lehmann, 2021; Vonopartis et al., 2021). The pressure produced by sudden expulsion of large vol- umes of water vapor from the final silicate magma can cause widespread cracking of both the granite roof and adjacent rocks, which allows the escape of metal-bearing hydrothermal fluids (Lehmann, 2021). This is why fluorite and the boron mineral tourmaline are very often associated with cassiterite in hydrothermal veins. African A-type (anorogenic) granites that lack significant amounts of fluorite and tourmaline also lack economic tin mineralization (Vonopartis et al., 2021: 16). Tin is soluble in reduced solutions as Sn2+ but is precipitated by oxidation to Sn4+, forming crystals of cassiterite (SnO ). 2 As we now understand, the drivers for tin isotopic fractionation in nature are divided into two stages that relate to (1) the segregation of reduced (Sn2+) tin into either the melt or water (hydrothermal) phases of a granite magma and (2) the pre- cipitation of oxidized cassiterite minerals, either in association with the granite plu- ton (pegmatite deposits) or in the hydrothermal veins that explode outward from its roof (Mathur et al., 2025). Tin isotopic fractionation in the first stage is driven by how much tin remains in the magma versus hydrothermal fluid, as the complexation of Sn2+ with the ligands F− and Cl− leads to significant enrichment in heavy tin iso- topes in the hydrothermal fluid (Sun et al., 2022). This relies on principles of equi- librium fractionation, where enrichment in heavy isotopes in one phase (resulting in a very positive δ124Sn signature) depletes the reservoir in these isotopes and leaves the light isotopes behind (resulting in a very negative δ124Sn signature). Modeling by Mathur et al. (2025) shows that a pegmatite with even 10% tin sequestered in the hydrothermal phase results in a predominantly negative δ124Sn signature and lowers the overall starting composition for cassiterite minerals. Following this first stage of isotopic fractionation, the second stage can be fur- ther subdivided based on two factors. These relate to (1) the required oxidation of Sn2+ to Sn4+ to mineralize cassiterite and (2) the creation of a vapor phase during fluid evaporation/boiling. The first of these factors concentrates the earlier formed cassiterite mineral with heavy tin isotopes, as compared to the later formed (and unexploited in southern Africa) stannite mineral (Yao et al., 2018). However, the Complementary Use of Lead Isotopes, Tin Isotopes, and Trace… Page 7 of 60 6 initial reservoir signature is critical in this step. If a pegmatitic reservoir has already been depleted in heavy tin isotopes based on their segregation to a hydrothermal phase (even if this phase is minimal), then the isotopic signature of cassiterite from this pegmatite will still be predominantly negative as the heaviest of tin isotopes have already been removed from the system. For a hydrothermal deposit, cassiterite signatures will trend strongly positive, and new evidence shows that earlier formed cassiterite has a heavier tin isotopic signature than later generations of cassiterite mineralization (Liu et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022). The second of the above factors suggests that deposits with a vapor phase exhibit more variable, yet still positive, δ124Sn data, as some of the heavy tin is sequestered into the short and strong Sn-Cl bond during the formation of the gaseous S nCl molecule (Wang 4 et al., 2019). Deep and slowly mineralizing pegmatite deposits do not form a vapor phase, and so this second factor only impacts shallow hydrothermal deposits. The resulting framework for tin isotopic fractionation in nature can therefore be divided as follows. Pegmatitic cassiterite will primarily have a negative δ124Sn iso- topic signature, even though the required oxidation of Sn2+ to S n4+ enriches cassit- erite with whatever heavy isotopes remain. This is because equilibrium fractionation has sequestered most heavy tin into the hydrothermal phase, even if this phase is minimal. Hydrothermal cassiterite, conversely, will have a low to strongly positive δ124Sn signature because of heavy isotopic enrichment by hydrothermal ligands and the oxidation of Sn2+ to Sn4+. Cassiterite in unaltered granite batholiths, meanwhile, will have values near 0‰, consistent with the signature of the host rock. These geo- logically driven fractionation mechanisms demonstrate that tin isotopes are an excel- lent predictor for the type of mineralizing environment: pegmatitic or hydrothermal. Background: Trace Elements in Cassiterite and Tin Metal Trace element concentrations in tin objects can reflect both the type of primary tin deposit (pegmatite versus hydrothermal) as well as distinguish between cassiterite mined from primary deposits (by hard-rock mining) and cassiterite recovered from secondary contexts (alluvial placers). The trace element composition of tin metal always differs from that of the cassiterite ore. Ore beneficiation and smelting tech- nologies determine which elements pass into the tin metal, which are lost as vapor, and which go into the slag (Chirikure et al., 2010). Iron (Fe) is usually the most abundant element after Sn in published analyses of ancient tin, but Fe concentrations are of no value for studies of tin provenance. Most of the Fe in tin likely derives from other minerals with which cassiterite is intimately associated in tin deposits, such as hematite, pyrite, iron tourmaline (schörl), and iron carbonates. Iron is undesirable in tin feed to a smelting furnace because it forms the intermetallic compounds FeSn and FeSn in smelted tin, which are difficult to 2 remove (Chirikure et al., 2010; Killick, 1991). As with tin isotopes, it is necessary to understand how tin ore deposits form in nature in order to interpret the abundance of other elements in smelted archaeological tin. In our above review of tin mineralization pathways, we note that incompatible elements are those which do not fit into the crystal lattices 6 Page 8 of 60 J. Stephens et al. for rock-forming silicate minerals and are therefore concentrated, with tin, into the remaining liquid (either as magma or hydrothermal fluid). These incompat- ible elements are mostly Large Ion Lithophile Elements (LILE) or High Field Strength Elements (HFSE) and are extremely important to identifying hydrother- mal versus pegmatitic tin and hard-rock versus alluvial tin. Tin and tungsten (W) are both classified as HFSE elements due to the ratios between their usual valences (Sn4+ and W6+) and ionic radii. The tungsten min- erals scheelite (CaWO ) and wolframite (Fe,Mn)WO are often associated with 4 4 cassiterite in both pegmatite and hydrothermal ore deposits (Černý et al., 2005; Heinrich, 1990; Hulsbosch et al., 2016; Lehmann, 2021). These oxides are much more difficult to reduce to metal than is cassiterite. (See free energy of formation ( Go) data for these compounds in Faure, 1998: Appendix B.) W was therefore f routed almost entirely to the slag during the preindustrial smelting of tin. This can be seen in analyses of tin smelting slag and metallic tin from archaeologi- cal sites near the Rooiberg tin deposit in South Africa. Slags from the Smelt- erskop archaeological site have W concentrations of 1300–5000 ppm (Chirikure et al., 2010), while W concentrations in 13 tin objects from South Africa are only 1–32 ppm (Table 1). Analyzed preindustrial tin slags from Southwest England contained 0.1–3.1 wt% WO (Malham et al., 2002; Tylecote et al., 1989) while 3 13 tin objects from the Bronze Age Salcombe Bay shipwrecks all have less than 14 ppm W (Berger et al., 2022a: Supplementary Material Table 1). Any W in metallic tin must be present as non-metallic inclusions. Tantalum (Ta) and niobium (Nb) both substitute readily for Sn in cassiterite, and pegmatite cassiterites often contain both elements at percentage levels. The absence of Ta in cassiterite from hydrothermal deposits is explained by the extreme insolu- bility of Ta ions in hot water (Lehmann, 2021). Go values for Ta and Nb oxides are f much more negative than that for cassiterite (Faure, 1998: Appendix B). They will not therefore be reduced by smelting, and should be routed entirely into the slag. Any Ta and Nb measured in tin artifacts must be present as non-metallic inclusions. Mn, Mo, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, and Ag are present in granites in much lower abun- dances than in mafic and ultramafic rocks (Faure, 1998: Appendix A11), and occur mostly as accessory sulfides. Conversely, Pb is more abundant in granites than in mafic and ultramafic rocks. All of these elements are concentrated, together with Sn and S, by the circulation of hot brines through the slushy roof zones of granite batholiths, and are then redeposited in cracks, fissures, and voids to form hydro- thermal sulfide vein deposits (Černý et al., 2005; Goldmann, 2016; Lehmann, 2021; London, 2008). The fact that tin ore deposits usually contain only minor quantities of Mn, Mo, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, and Ag is a consequence of differences in the tempera- tures of crystallization of their minerals from oxidized hydrothermal solutions. Cas- siterite and tungsten oxides are typically deposited from 600 to 400 °C in the roof of, or close to, the parent granite pluton. Most of the sulfides crystallize from 400 to 200 °C and thus are deposited further away from the margin of the granite (Černý et al., 2005; Robb et al., 2000). Where sulfides are present in tin deposits, they are usually the last ore minerals formed and thus may be spatially segregated from the richest lodes of cassiterite, or deposited in the very center of cassiterite masses that fill cracks or joints in host rocks. The magmas that produced the Lebowa Granite Suite (LGS) and Rashoop Granophyre Suite (RGS) were subsequently forced through the RLS along vertical fractures, solidifying above the RLS and under the Rooiberg Suite and Transvaal Supergroup rocks (Cawthorn et al., 2006; Nazari-Dehkordi & Robb, 2022; Robb et al., 2000). The entire BLIP appears to have been emplaced within a few million years, as all components of it have U–Pb dates on zircons of 2.05 Ga (Skursch et al., 2022). All tin mineralization in the BLIP is associated with the LGS, which cur- rently outcrops over some 30,000 km2, though much is still covered by younger rocks. Cassiterite is an accessory mineral in the coarse-grained and unaltered Nebo Granite, the oldest and most voluminous member of the LGS. Economic concentra- tions of cassiterite are found only at its roof, particularly in shells of the finer-grained Bobbejaankop and Lease granites, both formed by hydrothermal alteration of the Nebo Granite (Nazari-Dehkordi & Robb, 2022). Both altered granites contain con- centrations of cassiterite in pockets and pipes. Endogranitic tin ore deposits occur most notably in the Zaaiplaats tin field, with smaller deposits in the Stavoren–Mutue Fides (formerly Olifants) and Moloto tin fields (Kinnaird et al., 2016; Lenthall, 1974). Small pegmatite tin deposits have been noted in granites of the Mutue-Fides tin field and the Elands tin field. The latter is only 30 km east of the Rooiberg “A” mine. Evidence of Precolonial Tin Mining in Southern Africa In 1905, European prospectors discovered that long-abandoned mine workings at Rooiberg in northwestern South Africa (Fig. 1) were on tin lodes. Visiting geolo- gists left excellent descriptions of the old workings as these were reopened (Bau- mann, 1919; Recknagel, 1908; Trevor, 1912). There were at least six clusters of prehistoric mines, none deeper than about 30 m, in the Rooiberg tin field (Bau- mann, 1919; Recknagel, 1908). Those at the Rooiberg “A” mines, at the north end of the tin field, and at Leeuwpoort, 30 km south of this, were the largest. The most recent estimate by geologists of the extent of “ancient” mining in the whole Rooiberg tin field is that about 1000 metric tons of cassiterite were pro- duced from about 180,000 tons of mined ore (Rozendaal & Kellaway, 1988, cited in Grant et al., 1994). This estimate does not include alluvial tin placers, although there is clear evidence from analyses of precolonial tin slags that placer tin was also smelted (Chirikure et al., 2010). These placers were apparently exhausted before European prospectors arrived. Small copper-arsenic ore deposits in the Rooiberg valley (Hammerbeck & Schoeman, 1976) were also exploited before European colonization, as both copper-arsenic and bronze artifacts were found there by prospectors and farmers in the early twentieth century (Miller & Hall, 2008). Although the precolonial mines have almost all been destroyed since 1905, radiocarbon dates have been obtained on a wooden pit prop and on two charcoal inclusions in smelted tin. These all have calibrated age ranges between 1400 and 1640 CE, while charcoal trapped in an arsenical copper ingot at Rooiberg pro- duced a calibrated age between 1025 and 1285 CE (Grant et al., 1994). (All dates are at 95% probability). The only substantial tin smelting site in the Rooiberg tin fields (at Smelterskop) is much later. Ten radiocarbon dates from excavations at Smelterskop in 2006 and 2007 all fall in the broad range from 1650 to 1900 CE, which corresponds to a major plateau in the radiocarbon calibration curve (Chiri- kure et al., 2010). No other examples of precolonial tin mines in southern Africa have been con- firmed by archaeology. The well-regarded PorterGeo database of mine geology includes in its entry for Kamativi mine this sentence “Ancient Phoenician work- ings dating back some 2000 years are known at Kamativi.” (http://p orter geo. com.a u/d ataba se/m inein fo.a sp?m ineid=m n1537). The attribution to Phoenicians is obviously absurd, but the statement that there were precolonial workings at Kamativi deserves further investigation. We have not yet found an original eye- witness account that confirms the former existence of such workings. The geologist Martin Prendergast has argued that the hundreds of meters of trenches on Cornucopia Farm near Rusape, Zimbabwe were precolonial tin mines (Prendergast, 1979). These are associated with Zimbabwe-style stone walling and with thousands of “dolly holes”—rounded depressions in rock slabs formed by repeatedly crushing ore with a hammerstone. Dolly holes are reported in large numbers around gold mines in Zimbabwe, but Prendergast argues that the granites exposed at Cornucopia are much more likely to host tin than gold. Complementary Use of Lead Isotopes, Tin Isotopes, and Trace… Page 17 of 60 6 Unfortunately, no archaeologist has yet responded to his call to undertake exca- vations and no geologist has clarified if the granites around Cornucopia host tin, rather than gold. As noted in the previous section, there were placer deposits of cassiterite at many of the tin deposits in southern Africa when European prospectors first saw them. The exception is Rooiberg, even though there is evidence from slags that placer deposits were smelted there (Chirikure et al., 2010). Placer deposits at Rooiberg thus appear to have been exhausted before Europeans arrived. Placer tin deposits in other LGS tin fields were intensively worked in the early twentieth century (Crocker et al., 1976; Lenthall, 1974) so it is unlikely that evidence of any precolonial working of them now survives, except perhaps in smelting slags. There has been no search as yet for precolonial tin smelting slags around other LGS tin deposits. Prior Studies of Tin and Bronze in Southern Africa The rediscovery of the Rooiberg tin mines around 1905 coincided with the first excavations by a trained archaeologist in southern Africa. These were at Great Zim- babwe and at other major stone-walled sites on the plateau of Zimbabwe (Randall- McIver, 1906). Subsequent professional excavations (Caton-Thompson, 1931; Fou- ché, 1937) recovered copper alloys in association with imports from the Islamic Near East and India. These three published reports each included chemical analyses of a few samples of metal artifacts by professional metallurgists, and at each site some samples of bronze were noted. Few chemical analyses of metals from archaeo- logical excavations were made in subsequent decades. There was a revival of interest in the mid-1970’s with reanalysis of many of the tin and bronze specimens from earlier excavations (Friede & Steel, 1975, 1976) and the first professional archaeo- logical study of sites around the Rooiberg tin mines (Hall, 1985; Mason, 1986). In the early 1990 s, the archaeometallurgist Duncan Miller began systematic labora- tory studies of metals from archaeological sites. By the mid-2000s, he had shown that bronze was widely distributed across present South Africa and Botswana after 1400 CE (e.g., Denbow & Miller, 2007; Hall et al., 2006; Miller, 2001). These find- ings refocused attention on tin production at Rooiberg, and new surveys and excava- tions were undertaken there in 2006 and 2007 by a team led by Killick and Hall. A surprising finding of these new surveys was that there is very little evidence of tin smelting in the Rooiberg Valley (Bandama et al., 2013; Chirikure et al., 2010, 2023, 2024). Some evidence of tin smelting has also been found at sites 30 km north of the mines (Bandama et al., 2013), but there have been no other reports of tin smelting slags as yet from other regions of South Africa. Almost all of the estimated 1000 tons of cassiterite mined at Rooiberg are still unaccounted for. Tin objects are rare in the archaeological record of southern Africa. Tin prills in smelting slags and primary smelted tin have been found only in the Rooiberg and Sand River valleys (Bandama et al., 2013; Friede & Steel, 1976; Miller & Hall, 2008). About two dozen cast tin ingots in several distinct shapes have been found in surface contexts in several locations across northern South Africa (Friede & Steel, 1976; Killick, 1991), but the only tin object recovered 6 Page 18 of 60 J. (2023: Online Appendix A) report trace elements (deter- mined by LA-ICP-MS) for 163 cassiterite crystals from Zaaiplaats, Leeuwpoort, and Rooiberg “A” Mine. Of these, 160 have < 0.6 ppm Pb. These data are misleading, as they were measured only on the 208Pb peak (Teimar Nazari-Dehkordi, pers. com. to DJK). 208Pb is produced by decay of 232Th, and Th is < 1 ppm in all but 3 of 163 measurements. All four Pb isotopes were however measured on the smaller sample of cassiterites used for U/Pb and Pb/Pb dating (Nazari-Dehkordi et al., 2023: Online Appendix B). In this dataset, average total Pb for the Rooiberg “A” mine sample was 31.6 ppm (n = 38; average U = 80.1 ppm); in the Leeuwpoort mine, average Pb was 21.1 ppm (n = 32; average U = 53.6 ppm); and for Zaaiplaats, average Pb was 6.7 ppm (n = 31; average U = 16.2 ppm). WP has calculated expected radiogenic 207Pb and 206Pb values from the U con- centrations in Nazari-Dehkordi et al. (2023: Online Appendix A) and the Pb-Pb geological ages obtained for the dating samples discussed above (Nazari-Dehkordi et al., 2023: Online Appendix B). The average calculated 207Pb + 206Pb for Rooiberg “A” is 60.0 ppm Pb (n = 54; average U = 158.8 ppm); for Leeuwpoort 22.0 ppm Pb (n = 55; average U = 57.0 ppm); and for Zaaiplaats 8.1 ppm Pb (n = 54; average U = 21.5 ppm). There are no comparable published Pb isotope data for other south- ern African cassiterite. Dittrich et al. (2019) report LA-ICP-MS analysis of Bikita cassiterite but do not provide the data, just U–Pb concordia plots. On present worldwide data for cassiterites (Powell et al., 2024: Fig. 1) the Roo- iberg “A” deposit has the second highest U concentration and the highest calculated Pb. The Leeuwpoort deposit has the 11th highest U concentration, but the second highest calculated Pb. Zaaiplaats has the highest measured Pb and third highest cal- culated Pb (Powell et al., 2024: Fig. 5), in spite of being far down the list of U con- centrations. In each case, the high Pb content reflects the fact that these deposits are among the world’s oldest tin deposits (ca. 2055 Ma). No geologist has yet offered an explanation for the extraordinarily high U concentration in Rooiberg cassiterite, but we suggest one. Both the Rooiberg and Leeuwpoort deposits are located in Pretoria Series quartzites of the Transvaal System. At the base of the Transvaal System lies 6 Page 30 of 60 J. Stephens et al. the Black Reef Formation, a thin conglomerate with extraordinarily high gold and uranium content (Fuchs et al., 2016). This is not exposed at surface in the Rooiberg valley, but neither is the LGS granite. It is widely agreed that tin-bearing hydrother- mal solutions from the granite made their way up vertical cracks through Transvaal System rocks, and we suggest that these solutions may have picked up U in passing through the Black Reef. At Zaaiplaats, where the tin deposits are in LGS granites at surface, the average U concentration in cassiterite is only 21.5 ppm, compared to 158.8 ppm at the Rooiberg “A” mine. This suggests that most of the U in Rooiberg “A” and Leeuwpoort cassiterites did not come from the granites. Discussion Our integration of lead and tin isotopes highlights the difficulty of identifying the sources of tin, and of tin in bronze. It is certainly much easier to do this in south- ern Africa than in Eurasia because we have several factors working in our favor: (1) there are large differences in geological age of tin deposits (3000 Ma, 2600 Ma, 2050 Ma, and 1030 Ma), which produce vastly different lead isotopic isochrons; (2) tin isotopic ratios allow us to distinguish hydrothermal tin deposits from pegmatite tin deposits; and (3) there is a long history of research on the only known center of precolonial tin mining at Rooiberg (e.g., Baumann, 1919; Chirikure et al., 2010, 2023, 2024; Molofsky et al., 2014; Recknagel, 1908; Trevor, 1912) that provides us with clear understandings of the technology of tin mining and smelting, dates for the exploitation of the site, estimates for the amount of tin extracted, and hypotheses related to the social organization behind the production and distribution of tin. No Eurasian tin deposit mined in prehistory has as detailed a body of geological and technological studies. Lead isotopic, trace elemental, and tin isotopic data confirm at least one hydro- thermal source within the Lebowa Granite Suite for eight tin and Pb–Sn objects Complementary Use of Lead Isotopes, Tin Isotopes, and Trace… Page 47 of 60 6 (SA-1, SA-11A, SA-14A, SKRT1, 21/39/1, 21/39/3, B483, and Z334). We agree with Molofsky et al. (2014) that this was almost certainly Rooiberg, the only pre- historic tin mine yet known in the LGS. Prior chemical and petrographic analyses of slags (Chirikure et al., 2010) demonstrate that tin ore was won from both alluvial placers and from hard-rock mining. Trace element and tin isotopic data for the remaining seven tin objects provides the first evidence for the exploitation of tin deposits other than those in the Rooiberg valley. We infer that tin samples with negative δ124Sn values ranging from − 0.07‰ to − 5.64‰ derive from pegmatites, which are absent at Rooiberg, Leeuwpoort, and adjacent deposits. Chemistry from samples 14/47/1 and 14/47/2 indicates that one of these pegmatite deposits was polymetallic in type, suggesting a greisenized pegma- tite similar to those of Stavoren-Mutue Fides (Wagner, 1921). By integrating trace element, lead isotope, and tin isotopic data, we suggest that four objects (14/47/3, the tin lerale, and prill SEA-5 K) certainly come from a pegmatitic tin deposit in the LGS, possibly from the Elands or Stavoren-Mutue Fides tin fields. No archaeologi- cal surveys for mining or smelting sites have been made around either of these. Sample Z581 from Great Zimbabwe is unique in several respects. It is the only one with archaeological context and associated radiocarbon dates, and is also unique in having an anomalous (“post-modern”) model age with very high Pb concentration (1200 ppm). Prendergast (1979) suggested that it might have been made from peg- matite tin at Cornucopia in east-central Zimbabwe, where a carved soapstone mould for ingots of similar size and shape was found. Its δ124Sn (− 0.57‰) confirms that it derives from a pegmatite deposit, but its peculiar Pb character is best explained by mixing Pb from cassiterite with galena formed from Pb scavenged from some high- U mineral, likely during the intrusion of the Bushveld LIP. No Pb isotope ratios are yet available for galena in LGS tin deposits, so we cannot yet suggest a source—but it is not likely to have been in modern Zimbabwe. Like the results from the tin objects, data from archaeological bronzes predomi- nantly show signatures which align with the hydrothermal LGS tin deposit at Roo- iberg, though there are possible samples which could be consistent with other tin deposits. Importantly, we find no evidence to suggest that any of these bronzes was produced outside of southern Africa. Of the 153 bronze objects, we have ana- lyzed for lead isotopes at the University of Arizona, 120 had less than 200 ppm Pb and were potential candidates to detect their tin source with Pb isotopes. A com- parison of this assemblage of samples with isochrons for the major tin deposits in southern Africa shows that the LGS calculated isochron is certainly the best fit but also highlights some samples which deviate from the LGS calculated isochron and plot near the Bikita calculated isochron, or simply do not match any of the options (Fig. 8). Despite clear association with the LGS calculated isochron for six radio- genic samples above 30 on the 206Pb/204Pb axis, we also identify Pb mixing between this 2.05 Ga tin district and the 2.06 Ga Phalaborwa copper deposit. A sub-sample of 46 bronze objects with less than 200 ppm Pb, including five of these mixed Pb radiogenic objects, was selected for tin isotopic analysis. All of these have posi- tive tin ratios. We can confidently infer that samples with δ124Sn greater than 0.5‰ derive from hydrothermal LGS tin deposits, almost certainly Rooiberg (Fig. 2). Seven objects have δ124Sn values less than 0.5‰ and remain possible matches to 6 Page 48 of 60 J. Of these seven objects, Zim-Baranda-1 is by far the most convincing sample for a Bikita provenance as it also matches with the Bikita calcu- lated isochron. For samples with greater than 0.5‰ δ124Sn which deviate from the LGS calculated isochron, their lead isotopic data must be impacted by Pb mixing with their copper component during the bronze alloying process. This is best exem- plified in the Zim-Monk-3 sample where copper from the Copperbelt has pulled the LIA ratios off the LGS calculated isochron towards the Kamativi calculated isoch- ron (Killick et al., In Press). The integration of these two isotopic techniques demon- strates that much of the tin mined from Rooiberg was carried far north to be alloyed with copper for the production of bronze. Our analytical work has thus far docu- mented bronze at 33 different archaeological sites in South Africa, Botswana, Zim- babwe, and Zambia (Fig. 1B). Chemical analysis of these bronze objects is unfor- tunately not useful in identifying the source of tin, as trace element concentrations are contributed by both the tin and the copper components of the bronze alloy. The 208Pb/204Pb ratio is potentially useful in identifying the source of copper. 232Th is the parent isotope for 208Pb but has very low concentrations in cassiterite because it is not soluble in the highly oxidized fluids carrying tin; this isotopic ratio is therefore dominated by the copper component. We will discuss these additional lines of evi- dence in future papers, but for the present we conclude that the wide range of object chemistry and 208Pb/204Pb ratios implies that tin was mixed with copper from many different sources. The data presented here do confirm that tin deposits of the LGS in South Africa were the major source for tin in the larger region. We do however have to confront a seeming contradiction. Almost half of the tin samples analyzed have negative δ124Sn, and thus are clearly identified with pegmatite deposits, but not a single one of the 46 bronzes has negative δ124Sn. What can this mean? We think that it is sig- nificant that all but one of the tin samples are either tin ingots found on the sur- face or prills from smelting sites that date to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries AD. The Great Zimbabwe tin ingot Z-581 is the exception; it is dated by association with radiocarbon dates to the fifteenth or sixteenth century. All of the 46 bronzes for which we have both tin isotope data and radiocarbon dates are earlier, ranging from the thirteenth century (Mapungubwe) through the seventeenth (Khami, Thu- lamela). This could mean that the pegmatite tin sources were not used before the fif- teenth–sixteenth centuries. (We are probably safe in assuming that tin ingots found on surface were among the last to be produced). But we only have Sn isotope data for 46 of 153 bronzes: future analysis may find that some of the bronzes yet unana- lyzed will have negative δ124Sn values. Chirikure et al. (2023, 2024) pair the lack of evidence for tin smelting with the wide variation in Complementary Use of Lead Isotopes, Tin Isotopes, and Trace… Page 49 of 60 6 tin ingot morphology to argue that the Rooiberg tin deposits in northern South Africa were open resources, available to anyone who wanted to mine and smelt tin. The variety of ingot shapes matching tin-bearing pegmatites in the BLIP (the horned 14/47/3 ingot and the tin lerale) show that this was a wider phenomenon which included the whole BLIP. The tin bar Z581 and the skinny tin rods 14/47/1 and 14/47/2 possibly can be included in this statement, but we simply do not have enough evidence to infer a probable source. Like evidence from Rooiberg, minerals were likely transported away from their alluvial placers and smelted elsewhere. Prill SEA-5 K shows that this was the case, and that some pegmatitic placer tin was trans- ported to the Elandsberg ledge site, in the Rooiberg valley, for smelting. Evidence from the bronze samples also demonstrates that tin mined at Rooiberg was carried far away and combined with copper from multiple sources. We will discuss our evi- dence for copper sources in bronzes in other publications. The chemical composi- tion of copper from the Copperbelt and from Kipushi is discussed in Stephens et al. (2023a) and Killick et al. (In Press) identify copper from the Central African Cop- perbelt, Kipushi, Kabwe, and an unknown Zimbabwean Greenstone Belt deposit in bronze samples from Ingombe Ilede (Zambia) and at Monks Kop and Castle Kopje (both in northern Zimbabwe). Publications on the sources of copper in bronzes from Botswana are in preparation. As noted above, 208Pb/204Pb ratios in bronze usually point to copper sources, but more useful still are systematic variations in chemistry between deposits. For example, copper from the northern Rooiberg valley and from Copper Queen mine in northern Zimbabwe contains relatively high levels of arsenic and antimony, while nickel at levels from thousands of ppm to percentages is char- acteristic of the Vlakfontein pipes in South Africa and of the Phoenix and Selkirk mines in Botswana. While the assemblage of bronze items presented here demonstrates that this alloy was a much more common feature of the archaeological record of southern Africa, its presence (or absence) in certain areas helps us to understand regional interac- tion. Sites with bronze are noted throughout Zimbabwe, along the eastern margin of Botswana between the modern cities of Palapye and Francistown (where a number of large precolonial sites and copper mines were located) and in Zambia at the lone site of Ingombe Ilede. We have recently sampled extensively from sites in South Africa, including (as suggested by Bandama, 2013: 189) a time series of sites in the Limpopo valley from the ninth through the thirteenth centuries, to determine when bronze first appears in the archaeological record. We have no answer as to why there is as yet no sign of bronze in sites in Zambia (except for Ingombe Ilede), or in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). It is remarkable that copper ingots were car- ried in large numbers from the Copperbelt to Zimbabwe (Stephens et al., 2023a, b) but that no tin or bronze seems to have gone from Zimbabwe to the Copperbelt or to the DRC. Perhaps the adoption of bronze arose as a consequence of changing prefer- ences as the Limpopo valley, eastern Botswana, and present Zimbabwe developed more frequent interaction with the Indian Ocean trading network coming from the Swahili coast? On present evidence, the Indian Ocean network did not extend much beyond the Zambezi river valley into Zambia. While some evidence for glass beads, shell, and other materials originating from the east coast certainly exists at sites in southern Zambia (e.g., Pawlowicz et al., 2020), there is hardly any evidence of 6 Page 50 of 60 J. The first gold and the first bronze in southern Africa, on present evidence, appear together at Mapungubwe in the thirteenth century. We have considered whether the adoption of bronze was in imitation of gold, but the lack of consistency in the tin content of bronzes (Figs. 9 and 10) argues against this proposition. Conclusion Although sub-Saharan Africa is well endowed with tin deposits (Kinnaird et al., 2016), tin appears to have been mined in only two regions before European coloni- zation (Killick, 2016). These are the Rooiberg tin field and the Jos plateau of Nigeria (Fell, 1939). Almost nothing is known about the origins of tin and bronze in Nigeria, but their first use must predate the exquisite cast tin bronzes at Igbo Ukwu (Shaw, 1970), which were produced somewhere between the tenth and thirteenth centuries CE (McIntosh, 2022). The earliest bronze in southern Africa made with local tin dates to the thirteenth century, at Mapungubwe. Why did tin and bronze appear so late in sub-Saharan Africa? The smelting of tin from cassiterite is no more difficult than the smelting of iron, which had been prac- ticed since at least 500 BC in West Africa, and in southern Africa from around 300 CE. Imports from the Muslim world, especially glass beads, appeared in northern South Africa by the ninth century, but on present evidence there was no use of tin, 6 Page 54 of 60 J. Stephens et al. bronze, or gold before the thirteenth century (Killick, 2016). Was Rooiberg the only tin district mined in precolonial southern Africa? And what happened to the large quantity of tin produced at Rooiberg? The first question cannot yet be answered, but this article addresses the second and third questions. JSON: Name: integrated_isotope_trace_pipeline Title: An integrated pipeline using lead isotopes, tin isotopes, and trace-element fingerprints to assign geological provenance of tin in precolonial southern African bronzes Short Hypothesis: For archaeological bronze objects with bulk Pb concentration ≤150 ppm, jointly using tin isotope composition (δ124Sn), lead isotope ratios (206Pb/204Pb, 207Pb/204Pb, 208Pb/204Pb), and trace-element patterns will discriminate hydrothermal Lebowa Granite Suite (LGS) tin from pegmatitic tin sources with at least 85% classification accuracy. Related Work: Prior approaches have used single or paired isotope systems (lead isotopes alone or tin isotopes in isolation) and trace-element fingerprints to infer tin provenance. Lead-isotope studies exploit radiogenic Pb from old cassiterites but are confounded when copper in a bronze contributes substantial Pb or when cassiterite U/Th heterogeneity and accessory minerals introduce excess Pb. Tin-isotope studies (δ124Sn) can distinguish hydrothermal versus pegmatitic cassiterite but often lack sufficiently large or geographically representative cassiterite baselines and do not systematically account for smelting or post-depositional fractionation. Trace-element approaches identify deposit-type indicators (e.g., In, W, Ta, Nb, REE) but are limited because many elements partition to slag or occur as non-metallic inclusions, and they can be dominated by copper-source signatures in bronze. Existing methods therefore suffer from (1) ambiguity when Pb isotopic isochrons overlap among deposits, (2) lack of quantitative thresholds for when tin dominates a bronze's Pb signature, (3) insufficient integrated workflows combining Pb isotopes, tin isotopes, and multi-element chemistry, and (4) limited experimental validation using synthetic mixtures and copper-source baselines. Abstract: We propose a structured analytical pipeline that integrates lead isotope ratios, tin isotope compositions, and multi-element trace chemistry to assign the geological provenance of tin in archaeological bronzes from southern Africa. The pipeline combines (1) a measured baseline of cassiterite from candidate deposits, (2) precise Pb isotope isochron/mixing modelling that accounts for in-situ radiogenic growth, (3) δ124Sn-based discrimination between hydrothermal and pegmatitic ore types, and (4) trace-element patterns to detect placer inputs and non-metallic inclusions. We will test quantitative Pb concentration thresholds that determine when a bronze’s lead isotopic signal is tin-dominated versus copper-dominated, and implement Bayesian mixing models to apportion Pb sources and recover tin provenance probabilities. The main contribution is a validated, reproducible protocol that yields probabilistic source attributions and estimates of mixing, enabling robust mapping of tin circulation networks. Expected outcomes include an operational Pb cutoff for provenance, performance metrics for combined isotopic assignments, and a provenance dataset for southern African bronzes that refines models of precolonial metal exchange. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Archaeological metals: all available bronzes (n ≈ 153), tin ingots/prills (n ≈ 13), and Pb–Sn alloy curiosities (n = 2) as reported in the source corpus; (B) Geological baseline: cassiterite single-grain analyses from candidate deposits (Bikita, Benson, Kamativi, Rooiberg A and Leeuwpoort, Zaaiplaats, Stavoren/Mutue-Fides, Elands) n ≈ 43; (C) Copper-source baseline: sulfide copper ores and archaeological copper from major copper provinces (Central African Copperbelt, Phalaborwa, Kipushi, local Zimbabwean greenstone belt) n ≈ 100. Measurements: Pb isotopes (204,206,207,208) by MC-ICP-MS; δ124Sn and δ120Sn by MC-ICP-MS double-spike; trace elements by solution ICP-MS (bulk digestion). Baselines and calibration: measure U, Th, Pb concentrations in cassiterite baseline to compute radiogenic Pb expectations and construct calculated isochrons (Stacey–Kramers two-stage model) for each deposit. Experimental pipeline and comparisons: 1) Determine bronze bulk Pb concentration distribution; 2) Define Pb concentration cutoffs to test: 25, 50, 100, 150, 200 ppm; 3) For each cutoff, partition bronzes into candidates where tin-dominated Pb is possible; 4) Provenance assignment methods (baselines): (a) Pb-only isochron matching (nearest isochron or Bayesian fit), (b) δ124Sn-only classification (threshold classifier: δ124Sn >0.5‰ = hydrothermal, δ124Sn ≤0 = pegmatite), (c) trace-elements-only multivariate classifier (Random Forest on trace matrix), (d) combined method: Bayesian hierarchical model that uses Pb isotopes, δ124Sn, and multivariate trace data to produce posterior probabilities for each deposit; 5) Synthetic validation: construct 1000 simulated bronze mixtures by combining measured cassiterite Pb and Sn signature(s) with measured copper Pb signatures at defined proportions (tin mass fractions from 1% to 30%), add analytical noise, and test classifier recovery of true tin source and mixing proportions; 6) Ablation studies: (I) remove tin isotopes, (II) remove trace elements, (III) vary Pb-cutoff thresholds to quantify effect on assignment accuracy, (IV) remove copper-source baseline to test sensitivity; 7) Cross-validation: k-fold cross-validation (k=10) on archaeological set where provenance is independently constrained (e.g., modern smelter ingots SA-1, SA-2) and on synthetic mixtures; 8) Metrics: classification accuracy, precision, recall, F1 per source; confusion matrix; RMSE and bias for estimated tin fraction in mixing model; MSWD for fitted isochrons; posterior entropy and credible intervals for source probabilities; significance testing by permutation test (n=10,000) comparing combined method to Pb-only baseline. Reporting: report the Pb cutoff that maximizes correct tin-source classification and quantify confidence intervals on assigned sources for all archaeological bronzes. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Baseline incompleteness: un-sampled or unknown tin deposits could produce signatures not represented in the baseline and lead to misassignments. 2) Cassiterite heterogeneity: within-deposit U/Th, Pb, and δ124Sn heterogeneity can violate single-isochron assumptions and inflate MSWD values. 3) Smelting and metallurgical effects: variable loss of light isotopes, segregation of trace elements to slag or inclusions, and capture of accessory minerals in metal can modify bulk signatures, limiting direct cassiterite→metal comparisons. 4) Lead mixing with copper: when copper contains >150–200 ppm Pb or when copper Pb is highly radiogenic and age-similar to deposit Pb, Pb isotopes will be dominated by copper and tin provenance becomes ambiguous. 5) Analytical constraints: destructive sampling limits sample sizes; LA-ICP-MS spot analyses may not reflect bulk composition; small sample mass can increase measurement uncertainty for δ124Sn. 6) Modeling assumptions: reliance on Stacey–Kramers two-stage evolution, chosen priors in Bayesian models, and linear mixing assumptions may not capture complex multi-stage geological histories. 7) Archaeological biases: sample preservation, selective recovery of object types, and potential recycling/recasting of metal produce population-level biases that limit generalizability. 8) Scalability: high-precision isotopic analyses (MC-ICP-MS, double-spike) are resource-intensive, limiting throughput and replication.
